title: Reka AI Pricing 2026: API Models and Vision Costs
summary: Reka AI pricing compared to ChatGPT, Claude, and others shows you which service offers the best value for your needs. See how prices break down by token.
body_markdown:
## Hidden costs and limits teams hit with Reka


Those document sizes will understate your bill. You also have to count output tokens, retries, re-processed video and throttling, none of which show up when you multiply input volume by a listed rate.


### Output tokens and long prompts


A workload that generates long answers costs more per request than the same workload returning short labels, because output tokens are priced above input tokens. A summarization job and a classification job over identical documents will land on very different bills.


Estimate the output length per call, not just the document size.


Long-context prompts add a second layer. If you resend the same large document with every question, you pay for those input tokens on every call. A chat interface that replays a growing history does the same thing, and the cost climbs with each turn.


Retries belong here too. A timeout or malformed response that you re-run bills the whole prompt again, so a modest failure rate quietly inflates the total.


### Video re-processing and storage


Because video is billed on duration, anything that makes you process the same footage twice is a direct cost. Changing your index settings, fixing a bad ingest, or switching what you extract can all force a re-index of the whole library.


Budget for at least one full re-run before you trust a one-time ingestion number.


Storage is a separate question from processing. Before committing, ask whether indexed video is kept for a fee, how long it stays, and whether Vision plans carry minimums or per-seat charges.


### Reka throttling and plan rate ceilings


Every plan has a requests-per-minute ceiling, and a batch job that ignores it won't fail cleanly. **Requests above the cap get rejected or delayed** , and your retry logic then sends them again.


[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) prices the run, not the steps inside it: a flow costs 1 credit whether it has two steps or ten, so a Reka job split into fetch, call, validate, retry and log costs what the single lumped step did.


Zapier's per-task billing and Make's per-module billing, as their own pricing pages state, charge more for that same split, which taxes the very discipline that keeps a throttled batch reliable. Only Reka's meter then moves with the work you send.


Peak hours are where this bites. A workload that averages comfortably under the cap can still exceed it during a burst.


Size your estimate against the busiest minute, not the monthly average, and check whether the next plan tier is a sensible fix or just a higher floor.


Reka wins when your workload is video-heavy or multimodal and its models are good enough for the task. It loses when you need the widest model range or discount machinery you can verify on a public page.


### Multimodal API models: Reka vs Gemini vs OpenAI


They're Reka Edge, Reka Flash 3, Gemini 3 Flash and GPT-6 Luna, each taken from that vendor's own pricing page with its check date.


After the chart, compare on the dimensions that change a real invoice, in this order:


1. Whether each vendor has a free tier, and whether it covers the modality you use.
2. The rate limits at your plan level, since a throttled pipeline needs a bigger tier or a retry queue.
3. Whether a batch discount exists and which endpoints it covers.
4. Whether cached input is billed at a reduced rate for repeated long prompts.


Gemini and OpenAI publish these terms on their pricing pages, so you can fill in all four without talking to anyone. Where a Reka page leaves one of them vague, treat it as unknown and ask before you commit.


Each vendor is cheapest somewhere. Reka's small models suit high-volume multimodal calls where quality needs are modest. Gemini Flash suits very long inputs. GPT-6 Luna suits high-volume text work. Your own token counts decide among them.


### Video understanding: Reka Vision vs Twelve Labs


Reka Vision is Reka's product for searching and analysing video. Twelve Labs is a company that builds video understanding models and sells them through its own API.


Because Reka Vision and Twelve Labs are billed on different bases, a per-token price can't be set directly against a per-video-minute price. You have to convert one into the other using your own average clip length and how often you re-analyse the same footage.


If you index a library once and query it many times, the one-off processing cost matters less than the cost of each query. If you re-process footage regularly, the processing price dominates and storage or indexing fees matter less.


Reka is the stronger choice if you're already using its models elsewhere and want one vendor and one invoice. Twelve Labs is the safer choice if video search is the whole product and you want a vendor whose pricing is built around that unit.


Run one representative day of footage through both before you choose.
